steps.body: Some shapes lie flat on paper; others take up space you can hold. The drawn circle is FLAT; the ball is SOLID.
steps.narration: Some shapes lie flat on paper; others take up space you can hold. The drawn circle is FLAT; the ball is SOLID.

widget.prompt: Measure a longer edge of the box. Start at zero and cover it with 6 equal unit blocks.
widget.successFeedback: 6 equal blocks cover the longer box edge exactly.
widget.alignFeedback: Line up zero with the object's starting end before measuring.
widget.gapOverlapFeedback: The blocks must touch end to end — no spaces and no covering the same part twice.
widget.unitFeedback: Every block must be the same size, or the count means nothing.

predict.prompt: A ball and a drawn circle — which can your hand pick up?

options.label: The ball — it takes up space

predict.reveal: The drawing stays on its page; the solid has an inside for your hand to grasp.

cml.actionGoal: Name shapes by sides and corners, place them with position words, and compose them edge to edge for kgb flat solid.
invariants: A shape's name lives in its sides and corners — not its size, pose, or color; position words compare a thing to a landmark; and shapes joined edge to edge compose a larger whole — the anchors for kgb flat solid.
misconceptions: Renaming a turned or resized shape, using position words without a landmark, or treating shapes as unjoinable.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the shape were turned upside down, which of its sides or corners would disappear?

widget.prompt: What separates a FLAT shape from a SOLID shape?

options.label: Flat lies on paper; solid takes up space you can grasp
options.feedback: Correct — a drawn circle is flat, a ball is solid; the solid has an inside your hand can hold.

options.label: Flat shapes are smaller
options.feedback: A flat shape can be enormous and a solid tiny; the difference is space, not size.

options.label: Solid shapes are heavier
options.feedback: Weight belongs to material; a foam cube is light and still solid.

options.label: There is no difference
options.feedback: Try picking a drawn circle off the page — the ball comes, the drawing stays.

widget.prompt: Why can cans be stacked into a steady tower?

options.label: Their flat circle ends rest on one another
options.feedback: Correct — stacking needs flat faces meeting flat faces; the cans' circular ends provide them.

options.label: They are shiny
options.feedback: Shine is looks, not structure — a dull can stacks exactly as well.

options.label: They roll well
options.feedback: Rolling is the SIDE surface's talent; stacking uses the flat ends instead.

options.label: They are heavy
options.feedback: Weight without flat faces topples; the flat ends do the steadying.

widget.prompt: Tap the solid blocks that make the most stable tall tower.

hotspots.label: cones
hotspots.feedback: Cones narrow to points, so they do not make broad, steady layers for a tall tower.

hotspots.label: spheres
hotspots.feedback: Spheres roll out from under any layer placed on them; curves cannot hold a tower.

widget.missFeedback: Towers stand on flat faces meeting flat faces — find the blocks made entirely of them.
widget.successFeedback: Yes — a circle is round all the way, like a coin or a clock.

widget.prompt: Which solid rolls most easily because its surface is curved all the way around?

options.label: A sphere
options.feedback: Correct — a sphere has a curved surface in every direction, so it rolls easily.

options.label: A cube
options.feedback: A cube rests on flat square faces and does not roll smoothly.

options.label: A rectangular prism
options.feedback: Its flat faces catch the ground and stop the tumble.

options.label: A pyramid
options.feedback: A pyramid sits fast on its flat base and points stubbornly upward.
